prompt: A compact disc has the shape of a circle of diameter $5$ inches with a $1$-inch-diameter circular hole in the center. Assuming the capacity of the CD is proportional to its area, how many inches would need to be added to the outer diameter to double the capacity?

solutions.title: Double the area
solutions.body:
The area is $\pi\left[(5/2)^2-(1/2)^2\right]=6\pi$. For capacity $12\pi$ with outer diameter $d$: $\pi\left[(d/2)^2-(1/2)^2\right]=12\pi$, so $d^2/4=12.25$, $d=7$. We must add $7-5=2$ inches.

**Answer: 2 inches**

prompt: You have a list of real numbers, whose sum is $40$. If you replace every number $x$ on the list by $1-x$, the sum of the new numbers will be $20$. If instead you had replaced every number $x$ by $1+x$, what would the sum then be?

solutions.title: Find the length of the list
solutions.body:
Let there be $n$ numbers. Replacing each $x$ by $1-x$ gives sum $n-40=20$, so $n=60$. Replacing each $x$ by $1+x$ gives $n+40=100$.

**Answer: 100**

prompt: How many positive rational numbers less than $\pi$ have denominator at most $7$ when written in lowest terms? (Integers have denominator $1$.)

solutions.title: Count by denominator
solutions.body:
For each denominator $q$ count the numerators $p$ coprime to $q$ with $p/q<\pi$, i.e. $p<\pi q$:

| $q$ | range of $p$ | count |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $p\le3$ | 3 |
| 2 | odd $p\le6$ | 3 |
| 3 | $p\le9$, not multiple of 3 | 6 |
| 4 | odd $p\le12$ | 6 |
| 5 | $p\le15$, not multiple of 5 | 12 |
| 6 | $p\le18$, coprime to 6 | 6 |
| 7 | $p\le21$, not multiple of 7 | 18 |

Total $3+3+6+6+12+6+18=54$.

**Answer: 54**

prompt: In triangle $ABC$ with area $51$, points $D$ and $E$ trisect $AB$ and points $F$ and $G$ trisect $BC$. Find the largest possible area of quadrilateral $DEFG$.

solutions.title: Ratios of areas
solutions.body:
To get a large (convex) quadrilateral take $E$ between $D$ and $B$ and $F$ between $G$ and $B$, so $DEFG$ is triangle $DBG$ with triangle $EBF$ removed. Triangles with the same apex and bases on one line have areas in the ratio of the bases. Hence $\frac{[DBG]}{[ABC]}=\frac{DB}{AB}\cdot\frac{BG}{BC}=\frac23\cdot\frac23=\frac49$ and $\frac{[EBF]}{[ABC]}=\frac13\cdot\frac13=\frac19$. Therefore $[DEFG]=\left(\frac49-\frac19\right)\cdot51=\frac13\cdot51=17$. Swapping the labels $D,E$ (or $F,G$) makes the quadrilateral non-convex with smaller area, so $17$ is the maximum.

**Answer: 17**

prompt: You are given a $10\times2$ grid of unit squares. Two different squares are adjacent if they share a side. How many ways can one mark exactly nine of the squares so that no two marked squares are adjacent?

The numbers $112$, $121$, $123$, $153$, $243$, $313$, and $322$ are among the rows, columns, and diagonals of a $3\times3$ square grid of digits (rows and diagonals read left-to-right, and columns read top-to-bottom). What $3$-digit number completes the list?

solutions.title: Fill the grid
solutions.body:
The grid has $8$ lines (3 rows, 3 columns, 2 diagonals), and the list gives $7$ of them. The centre digit is the middle digit of $4$ lines (middle row, middle column, both diagonals), so at least $3$ of the given numbers have it as middle digit. The middle digits of the given numbers are $1,2,2,5,4,1,2$, so the centre is $2$. The top-left digit starts $3$ lines (its row, its column, the main diagonal), so it starts at least two given numbers; trying the possibilities, $3$ fails (only $313$ and $322$ start with $3$ and the remaining lines could not then supply $112,121,123,153,243$), so it is $1$. Then $243$ and $313$ must be the bottom row and right column (in some order), and the rest of the grid is forced:

$$\begin{matrix}1&1&2\\5&2&4\\3&1&3\end{matrix}$$

Its lines are rows $112,524,313$; columns $153,121,243$; diagonals $123$ and $322$. The only line missing from the list is $524$. (An exhaustive computer check confirms this is the only grid consistent with the seven given numbers.)

**Answer: 524**

prompt: Daniel and Scott are playing a game where a player wins as soon as he has two points more than his opponent. Both players start at par, and points are earned one at a time. If Daniel has a $60\%$ chance of winning each point, what is the probability that he will win the game?
If $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$ are integers, randomly chosen with the constraint $x+y\le10$, what is the probability that $x+y$ is even?

solutions.title: Group by $x+y$
solutions.body:
For $x+y=p$ there are $p+1$ ordered pairs, so the total is $1+2+\cdots+11=66$. The even sums $p=0,2,\ldots,10$ give $1+3+5+7+9+11=36$ pairs. The probability is $\frac{36}{66}=\frac6{11}$.

**Answer: $\frac6{11}$**

prompt: In a classroom, $34$ students are seated in $5$ rows of $7$ chairs. The place at the center of the room is unoccupied. A teacher decides to reassign the seats such that each student will occupy a chair adjacent to his/her present one (i.e. move one desk forward, back, left or right). In how many ways can this reassignment be made?

Several positive integers are given, not necessarily all different. Their sum is $2003$. Suppose that $n_1$ of the given numbers are equal to $1$, $n_2$ of them are equal to $2$, $\ldots$, $n_{2003}$ of them are equal to $2003$. Find the largest possible value of $$n_2+2n_3+3n_4+\cdots+2002n_{2003}.$$
